title: How to Connect Shopify and QuickBooks: A Complete Integration Guide
summary: Connect Shopify to QuickBooks Online to automate sales sync, reconciliation, and tax tracking. Compare methods and sync modes.
body_markdown:
Shopify and QuickBooks Online don’t connect natively, so every integration requires a third-party connector or manual work. U.S. e-commerce sales reached[$340.2 billion in Q2 2026](https://www.census.gov/retail/ecommerce.html) , up 12.2% year over year and 17.1% of all retail sales. Shopify merchants sold[$378.4 billion through the platform in 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1594805/000159480526000007/shop-20251231.htm) , and every dollar of it has to be recorded somewhere in an accounting system.


If you’re matching Shopify payouts to QuickBooks by hand, you already know the problem. A net deposit bundles orders, fees, and refunds into a single figure that matches nothing in your ledger. This Shopify and QuickBooks Online integration guide covers the three ways to connect Shopify to QuickBooks Online, the accounting gaps behind the mismatch, and how to sync Shopify and QuickBooks without losing transaction detail.


## **TL;DR**


- **No native integration exists:** Shopify and QuickBooks Online don’t connect out of the box – you need a third-party sync app or the official QuickBooks Shopify connector to bridge them.
- **Data sync covers far more than orders:** A proper Shopify QuickBooks sync brings across fees, refunds, discounts, taxes, and payment gateway splits, not just sales totals.
- **Sync mode determines your book structure:** Per Transaction sync gives customer- and product-level detail; Summary Sync posts consolidated daily entries – the right choice depends on your volume and reporting needs.
- **Shopify has unique accounting quirks:** Marketplace facilitator taxes, Shopify Payments payouts, and gift cards each require specific handling that generic connectors often miss.
- **Multichannel sellers need more than Shopify sync:** If you’re also selling on Amazon, PayPal, or other platforms, you need a tool like Synder that consolidates all channels, not just one.


## **Does Shopify integrate with QuickBooks?**


Yes, you can connect Shopify to QuickBooks Online, but not without installing something. There’s no built-in, toggle-on integration inside either platform that automatically passes your sales data between the two.


That gap exists for a structural reason:


- **Shopify** is built to run a store: it manages orders, inventory, customers, and payments.
- **QuickBooks** is built to run the books: it tracks income, expenses, accounts, and tax obligations.


They’re designed around different data models, different timing logic, and different ideas of what a “transaction” means. A Shopify payout, for example, is a net deposit that bundles together sales from multiple orders, minus processing fees, refunds, and any tax Shopify withheld on your behalf. QuickBooks has no native concept of that structure. Bridging the two means translating Shopify’s commerce data into accounting entries that make sense in a double-entry ledger, and that translation requires a connector.


The flow also runs one way: data moves from Shopify into QuickBooks, and nothing passes from QuickBooks to Shopify unless you add a separate inventory tool.


***Note:*** The question comes up in both directions, and the answer doesn’t change. Whether you ask: *can Shopify integrate with QuickBooks or does QuickBooks integrate with Shopify* , a connector is required either way.


## **Why Shopify revenue doesn’t match QuickBooks**


Five causes account for the gap between the revenue figure in Shopify and in QuickBooks, and each one traces back to how the payout was recorded. Shopify Analytics reports gross sales at the order level. QuickBooks reports whatever the integration posted. When the two disagree, the difference comes from one of the following.


1. **Net payouts booked as gross revenue.** Shopify deposits a net figure after fees, refunds, and any withheld tax. When that deposit posts straight to an income account, reported revenue is understated by the full value of the deductions, and none of the deducted items appear anywhere in the books.
2. **Processing fees not broken out.** Shopify Payments, PayPal, and Stripe each deduct their fee before the money arrives. If the integration doesn’t post those fees as separate expenses, the P&L shows no payment processing cost at all, and gross margin reads higher than it is.
3. **Marketplace facilitator tax double-counted.** Shopify collects and remits tax on Shop App and certain Shop Pay Installments orders on the seller’s behalf. Recording that withheld amount as your own liability overstates Sales Tax Payable, even though the cash never passed through your account.
4. **Payout timing crossing period boundaries.** Shopify Payments settles two to three business days after the order. An integration that posts on the payout date pushes end-of-month orders into the following period, which makes accrual-basis revenue wrong in both months.
5. **Refunds not reversed.** A refund reverses the sale, the sales tax collected, and the processing fee that Shopify Payments returns. When only the sale reverses, revenue corrects itself, but tax liability and fee expense both stay overstated.


A properly configured QuickBooks Shopify integration posts each component separately: gross sales to income, fees to expense, collected tax to liability, refunds as credits, and the net payout as a transfer. When every component carries its own entry, the Shopify figure and the QuickBooks figure resolve to the same number.


## **What transfers over from Shopify to QuickBooks**


Understanding what data transfers (and what doesn’t) is where most integration decisions go wrong. A Shopify payout isn’t a simple deposit. It’s a net figure that already has processing fees, refunds, and tax withholdings baked in. If your sync tool just posts the payout amount to your bank account, you’re losing the detail your accountant needs.


A well-configured Shopify QuickBooks integration syncs the following:


- **Sales revenue** – by product, order, or aggregated daily/period totals, depending on the sync mode
- **Processing fees** – Shopify Payments transaction fees or third-party gateway fees, posted as expenses
- **Refunds** – both the original sale and the reversal, so your revenue figures are net-accurate
- **Sales tax** – collected amounts mapped to your tax liability accounts or excluded if Shopify handles remittance directly
- **Discounts** – coupon codes and promotional discounts applied at the line level
- **Customer data** – names, email addresses, and order-level details (Per Transaction mode only)
- **Product and SKU information** – mapped to your QuickBooks items for COGS and inventory tracking
- **Payment gateway splits** – transactions via Shopify Payments, PayPal, Afterpay, or other gateways broken out separately


***What doesn’t move unless specifically configured* :** inventory asset values, COGS adjustments, gift card liabilities, and open invoice closures. Those require deliberate setup decisions, and they’re not handled by default.


## **Three ways to connect Shopify to QuickBooks Online**


How to integrate Shopify and QuickBooks comes down to three options, and each one balances control against automation differently. Every integration approach sits somewhere on the spectrum between control and automation. Here’s what each method actually delivers in practice.


### **Manual data entry**


You export Shopify reports, typically a payout summary or a transaction CSV, and enter the figures directly into QuickBooks. It gives you total control over what goes where and requires zero setup cost. But based on conversations with hundreds of ecommerce businesses, this approach becomes unsustainable somewhere between 50 and 200 transactions a month. At that point, the time cost, combined with the error rate from manual rekeying, outweighs any benefit from the hands-on control. One missed refund or miscategorized processing fee compounds across the month.


### **The official QuickBooks Connector (Intuit)**


Intuit offers an official connector app available in the Shopify App Store. It syncs basic order data into QuickBooks Online and handles some tax and payment information. It’s free with a QuickBooks Online subscription, reasonably straightforward to set up, and works well for stores with simpler accounting needs – a single payment gateway, no marketplace facilitator tax complications, and under a few hundred transactions per month. It doesn’t support advanced features like COGS tracking, Smart Rules, multichannel consolidation, or Summary Sync modes for high-volume stores.


Four conditions signal that the official connector has reached its limit:


- You sell on more than one platform
- You need COGS or inventory tracking inside QuickBooks
- You process more than roughly 500 orders a month
- Several payment processors pay out separately and you need reconciliation at the gateway level


Any one of these means rebuilding data by hand every month-end. Once those bookkeeping hours are priced in, a third-party accounting automation tool costs less than the manual correction it replaces.


### **Third-party accounting automation tools**


These are dedicated integration platforms that link Shopify to QuickBooks Online at a more granular level. They handle fee breakdowns, reconciliation, multichannel data, COGS, inventory, historical back-sync, and more advanced posting logic. The trade-off is a monthly subscription cost, typically ranging from a basic tier for low-volume stores to higher plans for high transaction volumes or multiple sales channels. ## **Choosing the right method**


The right choice depends on your transaction volume, the complexity of your chart of accounts, and how much reconciliation time you’re willing to absorb each month.


However, there’s a pattern that emerges most often – business owners can’t do manual bookkeeping as time pressure opens up a huge room for error.


Steven Freshour, CPA, founder of the ecommerce accounting firm The Seller CPA,[described the pattern in July 2026](https://www.sellercpa.com/blog/business-income-and-receipts-tax-compliance-starts-with-accurate-bookkeeping/) :


> Marketplace deposits recorded at the net amount instead of gross sales. Platform fees lumped together with revenue instead of tracked separately. Refunds that were never properly reversed. Income figures that don’t match anything the platforms actually reported. By the time those numbers made it onto a tax return, the damage was already done. Business income and receipts tax problems almost always start with the quality of the bookkeeping, not the filing itself.
>
>
> Steven Freshour, CPA, founder of The Seller CPA


What Freshour finds on those cleanups is a specific failure mode, and it’s more common than it sounds. When Shopify deposits hit the bank as a net payout (sales minus fees minus refunds minus tax withholdings), booking that deposit directly to income means the revenue figure is wrong, the fee expenses are missing entirely, and refunds never get reversed. The books look clean, but they don’t reflect what actually happened. The IRS receives 1099-K reports showing gross transaction volume from Shopify and its payment processors, so a return built on net deposits reports materially less than the platforms did, and that mismatch is what triggers the notice.


Manual entry errors show up in three places: a month-end reconciliation that doesn’t balance, a P&L with margins wildly different from what the business actually earned, and a sales tax filing built on net deposits instead of gross revenue. Each of those traces back to a shortcut taken at the data entry stage.


The only reliable fix is removing the manual step from the process entirely.

Their team spent 2-3 hours a week re-keying product data between the store and QuickBooks, and every hour of it was a chance to introduce an error. Automating the transfer with Synder removed the manual step altogether: they now report 100% accuracy in syncing sales data from Shopify to QuickBooks, and they save the equivalent of 12-18 full workdays a year on QuickBooks management alone.

## **Shopify-specific accounting challenges that every integration needs to handle**


A Shopify integration with QuickBooks Online has to absorb accounting quirks that most generic sync tools either handle poorly or ignore entirely. Getting these right in a QuickBooks integration with Shopify is the difference between books that reconcile cleanly and books that produce unexplained variances month after month.


### **Transaction and data accuracy issues**


- **Shopify Payments vs. third-party gateways** – Shopify merchants receive money from multiple sources: Shopify Payments, PayPal, Afterpay, Klarna, and others. Shopify Payments processed 65.6% of all platform GMV in 2025, or $248.1 billion, with 88% adoption among merchants in North America where the product is available, according to[Shopify’s FY2025 annual report filed with the SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1594805/000159480526000007/shop-20251231.htm) . The other 34.4% of volume moved through third-party gateways, each carrying its own fee structure and settlement schedule. Each gateway has its own payout schedule and fee structure, so deposits hit your bank separately. A proper integration breaks these down by gateway rather than lumping all Shopify revenue into one account. Without that separation, you’re reconciling blended deposits that don’t match anything in your bank feed.
- **Marketplace facilitator tax** – since 2020, Shopify collects and remits sales tax on Shop App and certain Shop Pay Installments orders on the seller’s behalf. That withheld tax shows up as a deduction in your payout – and if your sync tool records it as your own tax liability, your Sales Tax Payable in QuickBooks will be overstated. The correct handling is to record it as a pass-through line item that doesn’t add to your own payable.
- **Gift cards** – gift card purchases create a deferred revenue situation: you receive cash before delivering anything, so the amount shouldn’t hit your income account until redemption. Many integration tools record it as immediate revenue, overstating income in the period of sale.
- **Refunds and chargebacks** – every refund involves reversing the original sale and the associated fee. Shopify Payments returns the processing fee on refunds. If your integration only syncs sales, refunds have to be entered manually, and net fees will never balance. Operationally, a single refund requires three entries in QuickBooks: a reversal of the sale against the income account, a reversal of the sales tax collected against the liability account, and a credit for the returned processing fee. A chargeback reverses the sale but adds a chargeback fee instead of returning the original processing fee, so expenses increase while revenue decreases. Both fee types post to an expense account and are never netted against revenue, because netting them hides the real cost of payment processing inside your margin.
- **Payout timing vs. order date** – Shopify Payments typically settles 2–3 business days after the sale. If your sync tool posts transactions on the payout date rather than the order date, revenue lands in the wrong period for accrual-basis businesses – a problem that surfaces every time a reporting period closes mid-payout cycle. Here is the same problem with numbers. Five orders totaling $1,200 generate $38 in Shopify Payments processing fees, and one $45 refund is deducted from the same batch, so Shopify deposits $1,117. That figure appears in your bank feed as a single line, and no individual order in QuickBooks matches it, because the deposit is the net result of seven separate entries: five sales, the fee total, and one refund. How to reconcile Shopify payments in QuickBooks depends on the clearing account holding those seven entries, not on the order list.
- **Sales tax across multiple states** – Shopify collects tax based on your nexus settings, but those settings have to be correct for the downstream QuickBooks data to be reliable. If you’ve established nexus in multiple states, your integration also needs to map each state’s tax to the right liability account – not just post everything to a single Sales Tax Payable. That mapping is what makes Shopify sales tax sync with QuickBooks reliable, and it sets how to reconcile Shopify sales tax in QuickBooks at filing time.
- **Shipping income and costs** – Shopify charges customers for shipping and may partially subsidize it through Shopify Shipping discounts. If shipping revenue isn’t mapped to a separate income account, it inflates product revenue. If the subsidy isn’t tracked, your shipping cost picture is incomplete.
- **Bundles and kit products** – selling a bundle in Shopify that maps to multiple[SKUs](https://synder.com/blog/what-is-a-sku-number/) in QuickBooks requires specific product mapping logic. Most generic connectors either create duplicate items or fail the sync entirely when they encounter a product combination that doesn’t exist as a single item in the accounting system.
- **Multi-currency** – merchants selling internationally receive payouts in foreign currencies. Without multi-currency handling, exchange rate differences create unexplained variances in the ledger, and the clearing account never closes to zero.


### **How to sync Shopify with QuickBooks: choosing the right sync mode**


This is probably the most consequential configuration decision when setting up a Shopify QuickBooks integration, and it’s one most guides skip entirely. The two sync modes produce completely different book structures, and choosing the wrong one creates either data overload or a loss of the reporting detail you actually need.


Per-transaction sync is what lets you sync Shopify orders with QuickBooks individually, pulling every order in as a separate sales receipt or invoice. Customer names, email addresses, product names, SKUs, and line-level details all come through.


- **The upside:** you can run customer-level reports, track individual invoices, match open invoices to payments, and **run** a Shopify QuickBooks inventory integration that lets you sync inventory between Shopify and QuickBooks, so COGS and quantities update in real time with each sale.
- **The downside:** at scale, it generates a lot of records. A store doing 500 orders a month produces 500 sales receipts in QuickBooks, plus associated fees and refund transactions. At 5,000 orders a month, you start feeling it in QBO’s performance.


With batch journal entries **,** you get one aggregated entry per chosen period (typically a day), or per payout period for a connected platform. A Shopify store using Shopify Payments and PayPal would produce two entries per day: one summarizing all Shopify Payments activity, one for PayPal. Each entry is itemized by revenue, fees, refunds, taxes, and discounts, but contains no customer or product detail.


- The payoff is a clean, lean ledger that doesn’t balloon as volume grows.
- The cost is customer-level detail in QuickBooks, which matters if you need to track invoices by client or run product-level profitability reports.


***Practical guidance:*** if you’re doing fewer than roughly 1,000 orders per month and need customer detail or COGS tracking, per-transaction mode is built for you. If you’re a high-volume seller or an accounting firm managing multiple clients, consolidated journal entries are your right choice.


### **Multichannel operations**


Most Shopify sellers don’t only sell on Shopify. Based on sales consultation data from hundreds of ecommerce businesses, the most common setup is Shopify as the primary store, with Amazon or eBay as an additional channel, PayPal as a secondary payment gateway, and sometimes TikTok or Instagram feeding orders. Each of those channels generates transactions that need to land in QuickBooks.


The problem with treating these channels separately is that you end up running a different sync for each platform, managing five different account mapping setups, and reconciling five different deposit streams to your bank. It’s a wider pattern: in insightsoftware’s[Finance Under Pressure report](https://www.insightsoftware.com/lineos/blog/finance-teams-face-widespread-data-management-crisis-heading-into-2026-insightsoftware-research-finds/) from December 2025, 93% of finance teams named data management as a key challenge, 82% were running four or more separate tools for it, and 58% spent at least five hours a week moving data between systems.


The better approach is a single tool that connects all your channels, like Shopify, Amazon, PayPal, whatever else, and posts them all to the same QuickBooks file under a unified account structure. That way, your P&L captures all revenue sources in one place, your bank reconciliation compares a single consolidated ledger against your bank feed, and adding a new sales channel doesn’t require starting a new accounting workflow from scratch.

### **Recommended account mapping for Shopify data in QuickBooks**


Account mapping determines how to record Shopify sales in QuickBooks. Six data types come out of Shopify, and each one belongs in a different QuickBooks account type. Map them before the first live sync, because correcting account assignments after months of synced data means reclassifying every affected transaction one by one.


**Shopify data type** **QuickBooks account type**


**Product revenue** Income, with one account per sales channel


**Processing fees** Expense, kept separate from platform subscription fees


**Refunds** Income, posted as a credit against the original revenue account


**Sales tax collected** Liability (Sales Tax Payable), split by state where nexus applies


**Shipping income** Income, kept separate from product revenue


**Payouts** Bank, routed through a clearing account, one per gateway


The clearing account is what makes the payout reconcile. Gross sales, fees, and refunds post to the clearing account as they occur, and the net payout transfers from clearing to checking on the day Shopify deposits it. When that deposit appears in the bank feed, it matches the transfer exactly, and the clearing account balance returns to zero.


Account mapping is where most setup errors in a QuickBooks Shopify sync occur. If processing fees go to the wrong account, or if tax withholdings are double-counted, reconciliation will break every month until it’s fixed. It’s worth spending extra time here or[working with an accountant](https://synder.com/accountant-directory/) who has ecommerce experience.


## **What accountants actually say about QuickBooks for Shopify stores**


One of the questions that appears regularly around this topic is: *Why do some CPAs push back on QuickBooks Online for ecommerce businesses?* It’s a fair question, and the honest answer has nothing to do with QuickBooks being bad software.


QuickBooks Online was built around service businesses, freelancers, and traditional retail, not ecommerce operations processing thousands of transactions across multiple payment processors, platforms, and tax jurisdictions. Out of the box, it doesn’t understand the concept of a marketplace facilitator, it has no awareness of Shopify’s payout timing relative to order dates, and its inventory tracking (which requires a Plus plan or above) isn’t designed for the velocity and multi-channel nature of modern DTC brands.


Integrating QuickBooks with Shopify doesn’t remove that limitation on its own. The complaints from CPAs typically center on three things:


- The data volume problem (QuickBooks gets slow when flooded with individual sync records from high-volume stores)
- The lack of ecommerce-native account structures (you have to build them manually)
- The fact that any meaningful automation requires a third-party tool anyway.


Some accountants and business owners end up exploring[alternatives](https://synder.com/blog/8-best-free-quickbooks-alternatives/) : Xero for its cleaner multi-user experience and accountant-friendly interface, or enterprise platforms like Oracle NetSuite and Sage Intacct for businesses that have genuinely outgrown QuickBooks Online capabilities.


That said, for the vast majority of Shopify stores doing under $5 million in annual revenue and working with a QuickBooks-familiar accountant, QuickBooks Online is still a solid option. The data volume and complexity problems are solvable with the right sync configuration, specifically the Summary Sync mode that prevents the ledger from accumulating thousands of individual transaction records. The ecommerce-native account structure just requires upfront configuration work that most integration tools help you through.


## **Shopify QuickBooks integration: the bottom line**


Knowing how to integrate Shopify with QuickBooks Online is one of the most high-leverage accounting decisions a Shopify business owner can make. The integration itself is straightforward – the real decision is which method and sync configuration fit your business. The native connector handles simple setups well, but as transaction volume grows, payment methods multiply, and channels expand, a purpose-built sync tool pays for itself in hours recovered and reconciliation errors avoided.


Whether you frame it as how to integrate QuickBooks with Shopify or the reverse, the setup details that matter most are account mapping, marketplace facilitator tax handling, gateway separation, and choosing the right sync mode for your volume. Get them right at the start, and the monthly close becomes a review exercise rather than a recovery operation.


## **FAQ**


### **Does Shopify integrate with QuickBooks Desktop?**


Shopify integrates with QuickBooks Desktop through middleware, because Desktop has no direct API connection to Shopify the way QuickBooks Online does. A third-party sync app connects to both using the QuickBooks Web Connector, which is installed on the machine hosting your company file and pulls data on a schedule you define. Setup takes longer than the Online equivalent for that reason, and syncing runs on a schedule instead of continuously.[Synder connects Shopify to QuickBooks Desktop](https://synder.com/integrations/quickbooks-desktop/shopify/) in Per Transaction mode, recording each order individually with full product and fee detail.


### **Why use QuickBooks when Shopify keeps track of sales?**


Shopify keeps track of sales, and QuickBooks tracks the complete financial position of the business, which is a different job. Shopify Analytics reports what you sold and what you were paid, but it holds no record of payroll, rent, contractor payments, inventory purchases, loan interest, or owner distributions. Tax filings, loan applications, and investor reporting all require a P&L and a balance sheet assembled from every transaction in the business, not from the sales channel alone. QuickBooks produces those statements, and the Shopify integration supplies the revenue side of them.


### **Do I need QuickBooks Online Plus to use the Shopify integration?**


**A QuickBooks and Shopify integration doesn’t require the Plus plan for basic sales and revenue sync** – QuickBooks Online Simple Start or Essentials will connect to Shopify through most integration tools. You’ll need the Plus plan (or above) if you want to track inventory and COGS within QuickBooks itself, since inventory tracking is a Plus-only feature in QuickBooks Online. If you’re using Summary Sync and handling COGS in a separate inventory system, the lower QuickBooks Onlione tiers work fine for the accounting side.


### **How long does it take to set up a Shopify and QuickBooks integration?**


Most third-party sync tools can be fully connected, configured, and running test transactions within a few hours. The setup involves connecting your QuickBooks and Shopify accounts, mapping your chart of accounts, and configuring tax and product settings. A clean initial setup, especially with a complex chart of accounts or multichannel setup, may take a day or two if you’re working with an accountant to validate the mapping before enabling live sync.


### **How do I avoid duplicate entries when syncing Shopify to QuickBooks?**


Duplicate entries in QuickBooks come from two sources: two sync tools posting to the same company file at once, or a date range being imported twice. Disable the official QuickBooks Connector before you activate a third-party app, because both will post the same orders if they run in parallel. When importing historical data, check the last synced date first and set the import start date after it. Sync tools that include duplicate protection compare transaction IDs before posting, though that check only covers the data that same tool imported.


### **Can I import historical Shopify data into QuickBooks after connecting?**


Yes, most dedicated sync tools support historical back-sync, which lets you import past Shopify transactions going back months or even years. This is useful when you’re setting up the integration on an existing store and need your QuickBooks history to reflect actual sales. The date range and volume you can back-sync depends on the tool and the plan you’re on. For high-volume stores, historical syncs can take several hours to complete.


### **How do I categorize Shopify transactions and fees in QuickBooks?**


Shopify transactions categorize into four QuickBooks account types. Product revenue and shipping income post to income accounts, processing and platform fees post to expense accounts, sales tax collected posts to a liability account, and payouts post to a bank account through a clearing account. Refunds post as credits against the original income account. Record gross sales in income and never the net payout figure, since the net figure already has fees, refunds, and withheld tax deducted from it. For a full breakdown of Shopify fee types and the account each one belongs to, see[how to categorize Shopify transactions and fees in QuickBooks](https://synder.com/blog/how-to-categorize-shopify-transactions-and-fees-in-quickbooks/) .


### **What happens to Shopify gift card sales in QuickBooks?**


Gift card purchases create a deferred revenue situation: you receive cash but haven’t delivered the product yet, so it shouldn’t hit your revenue account until redemption. Most integration tools post gift card sales to a liability account and move the amount to revenue when the card is redeemed in a subsequent order. This is a configuration setting rather than automatic behavior – verify how your sync tool handles it during setup, because recording gift card sales as immediate revenue overstates income in the period of sale.


### **Do I need clearing accounts for multiple payment gateways?**


A Shopify store running several payment gateways needs one clearing account per gateway in QuickBooks. Each gateway settles on its own schedule with its own fee structure, so a single shared clearing account mixes deposits that arrive on different days and never closes to zero. Each clearing account collects the gross sales, fees, and refunds for its gateway as they occur, then the net payout transfers out when the deposit arrives. Sync tools built for multi-gateway stores create these accounts during setup and map each gateway to its own.


### **How do I troubleshoot Shopify and QuickBooks sync issues?**


Three checks resolve the common Shopify and QuickBooks sync failures:


**Sync errors that stop the process** – re-authorize the QuickBooks connection, because the access token expires periodically and has to be refreshed. The[Synder help center](https://synder.com/help/category/shopify/) documents the Shopify-specific settings behind each of these.


**Missing transactions** – verify that the sync start date covers the period and confirm every payment gateway is connected, since orders paid through an unlinked processor never enter the sync queue at all.


**Amounts that don’t match** – check whether the tool is posting gross sales with fees separated or posting only the net payout, and confirm the currency conversion setting for international orders.
